newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore December non-oil export data disappoints.
newsitem.headline: Singapore December non-oil export data disappoints.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil exports fell a disappointing 0.5 percent year-on-year in nominal terms in December after sliding 8.8 percent in November, the Trade Development Board (TDB) said on Monday.

The TDB said in a statement December's non-oil exports were worth Singapore $7.46 billion (US$5.33 billion). In real terms, the country's non-oil exports rose 4.6 percent in December to S$9.68 billion after falling 3.6 pct in November.
The figures confounded economists who had expected the figures to herald an end to the country's economic slowdown.
A Reuters poll of 15 financial institutions last week predicted a year-on-year rise of 2.9 percent in December in the non-oil export data.
"The numbers are definitely not as good as expected," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS/Standard and Poors in Singapore.
"But it is still an improvement from the slump in exports in November. The reason for this must be that the recovery in the electronics sector is patchy," he said.
The TDB said Singapore's total trade grew by 5.1 percent in 1996 to reach Singapore $361.5 billion.
It said the slower growth, as compared to 13.2 percent growth in 1995, was mainly due to a cyclical slowdown in global demand for electronics and related products.
All major trade components -- except oil trade -- chalked up lower growth rates, the TDB said.
Singapore's electronics and computer industries account for almost half its total industrial production and about 60 percent of its non-oil exports.

Its electronics sector grew rapidly through the 1980s and early 1990s but output slowed in the middle of last year in line with a global slump for electronics components. As a result, Singapore's economic growth slowed to 6.5 percent last year, from 8.8 percent in 1995.

Consumer demand for electronics began to pick up in the third quarter of 1996 in the United States but economists say it will still take another few months before the recovery has fed back up the supply chain to Asian producers like Singapore.
The TDB said total trade growth for 1997 was expected to be between five to seven percent.
Kaan Quan Hon, economist at DBS Securities in Singapore, said the recovery in Singapore's economy was still likely to take a while to take hold.
"We expect the recovery to get stronger as the electronics industry picks up in the second half of 1997," he said.
"On these figures, there is no evidence that we will get a strong recovery in the economy any time soon," he said.
